description: Team HELION is a high-school team from Edirne, Türkiye, joining the Ankara event (hybrid). We are three students, with skills in software, electronics, and design. We are building health monitoring software for astronauts on long space missions: it gathers health indicators and helps astronauts evaluate their health status and act on it in time. Our team is complete, but we are happy to connect with other teams and mentors!
summary: HELION is an active readiness self-test battery for astronauts on long missions. Using only a laptop camera, no sensors, no wearables, it runs four short tests (Physical, Memory, Social, Reaction), scores each 0–100, and produces one report with the weakest area highlighted and a concrete recommendation. It works fully offline: the camera models live on the device, results queue locally during communication blackouts, and the queued report is exported as a single file when the link returns. Two unscored companions, a Daily Log (water, meals, sleep, mood) and a Breathing Exercise, cover the day between tests.
details:
Try it live (no install): https://lordecaii.github.io/helion-astronaut-health-monitoring/
The astronaut app and the rater app are both linked from that page.

The story: Three Days Without Support

Two astronauts, Commander Kerem and flight engineer Arel, are on a Mars transit. One-way light time to Earth is 14 minutes. That morning a solar storm cuts communications completely: no contact with Earth for three days.

Their morning routine is the HELION battery, five minutes before breakfast. That day it shows: Arel's reaction score has fallen three days in a row, 82, 74, 58, his sleep is broken and he doesn't know it. Kerem's physical test flags strain in the knee-raise movement for the second day. The report's guidance is plain: rest before critical tasks; reduce load on the strained movement.

At noon comes the mission's most critical job: a course correction. Normally Arel runs that panel. With his reaction score down, the roles swap, Kerem makes the correction, Arel goes to a rest shift. The correction goes smoothly.

For three days there is no link to Earth, and HELION keeps working: the tests run on the laptop, the camera models are on the device, and every result queues locally, including the crew's written messages to the ground and their ratings of each other. When the link returns, three days of queued reports go to Houston as a single file. Arel's reaction score is back to 79 after rest; Kerem's knee strain never grew, because the load was reduced in time.

We did not rescue anyone at the last second. We caught the error and the injury before they grew. On a long mission, that is what survival usually looks like.

Impact

On Moon and Mars missions, crews of four to six spend months to years beyond real-time help from Earth, one-way communication delay reaches roughly 22 minutes at Mars, and blackouts can last days. In that setting, small declines matter early: NASA's Human Research Program notes bone loss of about 1–1.5% per month and treats isolation, distance and closed environments as standing risks to performance and behavioral health. HELION turns those risks into a daily, five-minute, crew-run routine: a falling reaction trend changes who makes a critical correction; a flagged strain changes the exercise load before it becomes an injury. Because everything runs and queues on one laptop, no monitoring day is ever lost to a blackout.

Creativity

  • Active testing, not passive monitoring. The astronaut performs the tests; the score is produced by performance, not collected from sensors.
  • Camera-verified movement. Physical exercises are counted by pose and hand landmark tracking, "I did it" is not enough; the camera confirms repetitions and holds.
  • Crewmate rating, by design. The social test is rated by a second person, never by the astronaut themselves. HELION ships as two apps: the astronaut app has no rating controls at all; the score is given from the separate rater app after the video call and transferred automatically. When Earth, the flight surgeon, is unreachable, the record waits in the offline queue for later transmission; it is never lost. The social module also has a "Send to Earth" panel: an astronaut can queue a written message about themselves, or rate a crewmate with the same rubric plus a free-text note, everything waits in the queue and is transmitted to the ground base when the link returns.
  • Offline-by-design. Models on device, results in a local queue, report exported as one file, the app assumes the link will fail, because on a real mission it does.
  • A visible trend, not a memory. The report graphs each section's day-by-day change from the queued records and marks declines in red, the three-day slide in our story is something the crew sees, not something they must remember. A free-text mission note to Earth queues with the same data and travels with the report.

Validity

HELION's tests are modeled on NASA's own flown instruments: the NASA Cognition battery (self-administered cognitive testing on the ISS) for Memory, and the Psychomotor Vigilance Test / Reaction Self-Test (flown on the ISS) for Reaction. The risk framing is NASA HRP's RIDGE model (The Human Body in Space). Scoring is transparent: Physical = completion minus 5 per strained movement; Memory = sentence recall + sequence score; Social = mean of five 1–5 criteria × 20; Reaction = click-time calibrated over 350–1200 ms. HELION is a readiness indicator, not a medical device: it does not diagnose, and it does not claim to measure radiation.

Relevance to the challenge

Self-assessment by the astronaut ✓ · camera-based, simple instructions ✓ · periodic (daily) measurement ✓ · improvement guidance in the report ✓ · color highlighting of the weakest area (red) ✓ · useful indicators from the challenge text, sleep and mood, tracked in the Daily Log ✓ · works with delayed or absent communication with Earth ✓.

How it works / technology

Plain HTML/CSS/JavaScript, runs locally (python3 -m http.server) or in the browser from the deployed GitHub repo (GitHub Pages). MediaPipe Pose Landmarker + Hand Landmarker run from local files in the app folder (no CDN at runtime). The social test uses WebRTC video with a lightweight signaling channel; the score arrives automatically over the data channel, no codes. HELION ships as two apps: the astronaut app, which cannot score its own user, and a separate rater app that only joins the call and scores. All data stays on the device (localStorage queue) and exports as JSON.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

The team used AI assistance (Muse and Claude Code) for software development, design iteration and text drafting during the event. All design decisions, testing and final content are the team's own, and every part of the system was tested and is explainable by the team members.
